sources.title: Carbonell & Goldstein 1998, The Use of MMR, Diversity-Based Reranking
sources.quote: "a linear combination of both criteria is optimized"; MMR "computes incrementally the standard relevance-ranked list when the parameter X=1" and "computes a maximal diversity ranking among the documents in R when X=0"; the paper suggests a value near 0.7 to focus on multiple overlapping/reinforcing relevant documents and a smaller value (about 0.3) for broad exploration.
sources.supports: MMR trades relevance against redundancy via a lambda parameter; lambda near 0.7 is a relevance-leaning setting (our '~0.7' is a heuristic consistent with, not mandated by, the paper).

sources.title: Broder et al. 1997, On the resemblance and containment of documents
sources.quote: "A contiguous subsequence contained in D is called a shingle." ... "the resemblance r of two documents A and B is defined as" [shared shingles over total distinct shingles]; "Hence the resemblance is some number between 0 and 1."
sources.supports: Shingle (contiguous word n-gram) overlap, as a Jaccard-style resemblance score, is an established near-duplicate measure; the 0.8 threshold and n=5 are our own tuning choices, not from the paper.

sources.title: RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Compression and Selective Augmentation (arXiv 2310.04408)
sources.quote: "an extractive compressor which selects useful sentences from retrieved documents"; "an abstractive compressor which generates summaries by synthesizing information from multiple documents"; "our compressor can return an empty string, implementing selective augmentation."
sources.supports: Extractive (sentence selection) and abstractive (model-generated summary) compression of retrieved documents are established approaches. Does not itself state the risks of dropped qualifiers or altered numbers.

sources.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (arXiv 2307.03172)
sources.quote: "performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context"; performance "significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts"; "current language models do not robustly make use of information in long input contexts".
sources.supports: Position of relevant information within the prompt affects answer quality, and extra irrelevant context can hurt.

sources.title: Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts (arXiv 2305.13300)
sources.quote: "LLMs can be highly receptive to external evidence even when that conflicts with their parametric memory"; "LLMs also demonstrate a strong confirmation bias" when external evidence partly matches their parametric memory, "despite being presented with conflicting evidence at the same time."
sources.supports: Models can be pulled toward parametric memory over supplied context in some conditions, but are not uniformly stubborn, so the override test is worth running rather than assumed.

sources.title: Koehn 2004, Statistical Significance Tests for Machine Translation Evaluation
sources.quote: "We call this method paired bootstrap resampling, since we compare a pair of systems." "create new virtual test sets by drawing sentences with replacement from the collection." "For each set, we compute the evaluation metric score for both systems."
sources.supports: Resampling the test items with replacement and scoring both systems on each resample (paired bootstrap) is an established method. Koehn derives significance from win frequency; the percentile CI on the mean difference is the standard analogous use.

sources.title: Berg-Kirkpatrick et al. 2012, An Empirical Investigation of Statistical Significance in NLP
sources.quote: "As might be expected, the size of the test corpus has a large effect." "the larger the corpus size, the lower the threshold for p-value < 0.05"; "the first 100 sentences of the Brown corpus have a threshold of 3.00 F1."
sources.supports: Small test sets need large observed gains to be significant, supporting 'the set is too small' for a 10-point gain on 40 queries.

sources.title: statsmodels docs: mcnemar
sources.quote: "If exact is True, then the binomial distribution will be used." "If the exact binomial distribution is used, then this contains the min(n1, n2)," where n1 and n2 are the counts that are zero in one sample and one in the other.
sources.supports: McNemar's test on a 2x2 paired table can be computed exactly with the binomial distribution on the discordant cells, matching our sign-test framing (the page does not use the word 'discordant').

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (arXiv 2306.05685)
sources.quote: "Position bias is when an LLM exhibits a propensity to favor certain positions over others." "Verbosity bias is when an LLM judge favors longer, verbose responses." Self-enhancement: "the effect that LLM judges may favor the answers generated by themselves." Swap method: "only declare a win when an answer is preferred in both orders" and "If the results are inconsistent after swapping, we can call it a tie." "Only GPT-4 outputs consistent results in more than 60% of cases." "GPT-4 defends significantly better than others" against verbosity. "Due to limited data and small differences, our study cannot determine whether the models exhibit a self-enhancement bias."
sources.supports: Position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases exist in LLM judges, vary across judge models, and the both-orders-agree-else-tie rule is a published mitigation. Self-enhancement evidence is explicitly inconclusive.

sources.title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators (arXiv 2305.17926)
sources.quote: "the quality ranking of candidate responses can be easily hacked by simply altering their order of appearance"; proposes "Balanced Position Calibration, which aggregates results across various orders to determine the final score".
sources.supports: Answer order alone can change an LLM evaluator's ranking; aggregating across orders is a mitigation.

sources.title: Length-Controlled AlpacaEval (arXiv 2404.04475)
sources.quote: "Despite being highly correlated with human preferences, AlpacaEval is known to favor models that generate longer outputs." "We introduce a length-controlled AlpacaEval that aims to answer the counterfactual question:"
sources.supports: Automatic judges can favour longer outputs, and length-controlled comparison is a recognised mitigation.
